newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Record Australian trade surplus underwhelms market.
newsitem.headline: Record Australian trade surplus underwhelms market.

text.p: Australia posted its best ever monthly trade performance in June, but the performance failed to stir economists or markets given the special one-off factors that drove the surplus into record territory.
The trade surplus jumped to A$1.964 billion in June, up from A$787 million in May, and the fourth surplus so far in 1997, Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) data showed.
The main factor behind the record surplus was the inclusion of A$1.8 billion in receipts from the first tranche of sales of gold reserves by the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA).
Earlier this month the RBA said it had sold 167 tonnes, or two-thirds, of its gold reserves.
The ABS said the remainder of the RBA gold sales will impact in August and September, when they will add another A$600 million to export receipts.
The improved trade surplus was seen having little impact on the market's current obsession -- a possible fifth interest rate cut -- and so given the special one off factors was largely ignored.

"Today's external account numbers provoked little interest and were essentially neutral for policy settings, with markets currently watching and waiting for a much heralded rate cut," Westpac senior economist John Peters said.
The inclusion of the gold sales saw exports of goods rise 23.2 percent in the month, while imports were up 9.2 percent.
Including services, total exports rose 19.7 percent, while imports were up 7.6 percent.
While the one-off factors have recently been all on the export side -- the May surplus included a A$500 million navy frigate -- imports had not fallen away, rising 6.2 percent over the quarter.
This strength in imports attracted some attention, with some seeing it as a sign of gathering strength in the economy.
"Imports are highly correlated with overall changes in domestic demand and can provide an early signal that economic activity is gaining pace," Colonial State Bank economists said.

However, the strong rise in exports over the June quarter -- the three month trade surplus was A$2.961 billion -- means that net exports will make a strong contribution to second quarter gross domestic product, data for which will be released on September 3.
The impact of the gold sales on net exports, will however, be offset exactly by a decrease in stocks and will therefore have no impact on GDP, the ABS said.
While having no impact on the national accounts, the gold sales will have a large impact on the quarterly balance of payments data which is due on August 28, economists said.

"With the monthly goods and services data for the June quarter now in, it looks like the current account deficit for the quarter will be at a 10-year low at around A$2.3 billion," Citibank Australia economists said in a commentary.
